"oMg ur fRoM gUaM???" Roughly 738,383 times I've heard this, between my first year at Stanford and my months in SF. I don't mind, though. It's kind of nice being the first person from Guam someone's ever met. 🇬🇺 But here's what I never get to say in those thirty-second conversations: Guam is where I transformed myself, quite literally and figuratively. I moved to Guam right at the start of 6th grade, and some of my classmates would ask where I was from and whether I could even speak English. I was overweight, not confident, and reserved until the pandemic. Maybe it's because Guam is so influenced by the military, I don't know, but my routine during COVID became as disciplined as an actual military schedule: wake up, eat, read books, study vocab, go out and work out for two to three hours, come back for family discussion, and sleep — on repeat. Actually keeping my promises to myself gifted me confidence. Soon after, I entered 9th grade and followed my older sister into JROTC. This essentially became the core of my high school experience. From staying back after school to train for fitness competitions, to standing for long hours in our perfectly ironed uniforms under the sun for ceremonies, to handing out letters to veterans on Veterans Day, to the countless hours we spent preparing for Army inspection. Gosh, this program truly shaped me. Beneath all of these events were the discipline, the teamwork, and the commitment. Looking back, I had the Army LDRSHIP values memorized in the back of my head throughout high school. Now, trying to write them out a year later, I can only remember half of them — but instead of cheating myself, I'll type out exactly what I remember: Loyalty, Respect, Selfless Service, Honor, Integrity, Personal Courage... just can't remember D, I guess lol. What I do remember, though, is how deeply one thing was ingrained in me: one drop of water is powerless, but together we are an ocean. Leading 200 cadets as Executive Officer by junior year, I truly learned how important it is to have everyone aligned on the same VISION and to lead by example. It was never "I'll check up on them when it's convenient." It was always "I'll help you from the very first step." And that is exactly why I am so obsessed with community building and human effort. Because I have SEEN with my own two eyes how a shy, reserved girl went on to become battalion commander four years later. Because I have SEEN how a guy I met freshman year, who was going through the hardest stretch of his life, later told me I inspired him to set goals and work toward them. He went on to join the Air Force. The years of effort, the days we doubted ourselves, the days we made breakthroughs, the endless emotions we overcame — THAT is exactly what AI cannot fake. And that is exactly why I am creating a passport of human effort @ commit.social . The website is live. Come leave your first proof of effort. 🌊

Grantmaking foundations should hire more staff with grant writing or nonprofit backgrounds. Hire people who have worked many a late night trying to get a proposal in on time. Who have fretted over repetitive questions in a grant application. Who have had to do so much with so very little. Who have tried to reach out to a program officer, only to find zero contact information anywhere. Who have panicked because a grant application calls for a specialized budget form, but the CFO is out of town. Who have been on the receiving end of a rejection email. We talk a lot about trust-based philanthropy and the things that make it – multi-year funding, simplified applications, shifting power back to grantees. Having worked inside foundations that practice this, I can say all of it matters. AND: trust-based practices are only as good as the people designing and running them. If you want a foundation that truly understands what applicants navigate day to day, hire people who've navigated it themselves. Their first-hand experience is invaluable, and it's exactly what this sector needs to actually change.

ADUs Are One of California's Most Successful Housing Programs. San José homeowners filed 1,806 ADU applications across 2023–2025 - 50 a month, on average, for 36 straight months. Through the hardest capital-markets stretch of this development cycle, while approved multifamily projects sat waiting at the financing gate, the ADU application curve didn't move. The geography is 29 ZIP codes, with the five busiest hold just 22% of the volume. This is parcel-by-parcel production across all single-family zoning districts citywide. The full breakdown of why the math works is now at https://lnkd.in/gTkRP7qj : → The two rulebooks: San José's City track (up to 1,200 sf) vs. the State track (800 sf, exempt from lot coverage and FAR) - the same parcel can pencil under one and fail under the other. → The 750 sq ft impact fee requirements: SB 543 made the impact-fee exemption inclusive (≤750 sf of interior livable space) as of January 2026. → California's first standalone ADU sale closed in June: $530K for a 749 sf two-bedroom near downtown, through the AB 1033 condo pathway San José adopted first. Plus two tools: a map of all geocoded applications, and a quick-screen calculator that runs track eligibility, fee flags, and gross yield on your numbers.

Seattle published a library of pre-approved ADU designs. Permitting doubled. Here's how it works: the city pre-clears ADU plans that already meet code, pass structural review, and include engineering. A homeowner picks a design off the shelf and skips the plan-check queue. The Pew Charitable Trusts studied 40 cities running similar programs. Results: - Permitting timelines drop by months - Construction costs fall $5,000-$10,000 per unit - Homeowners and small builders can actually participate Permitting costs and timelines are where ADU production stalls. Pre-approved plans remove that friction at the source. The cheapest housing policy any city can run.
